speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They ensure the safety and well-being of Singaporeans in a more dangerous, risky world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The demand for their work has gone up, but the number of those who do this important and often hazardous work has not.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In October 2023, I sought to understand the impact of the increased white-collar crime caseload of investigators from the hon Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I filed the Parliamentary Question after noting that the exponential rise of the sheer number of e-documents that these investigators have to parse through for each case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The rise in white-collar crime is an important sign of how the operating environment as a whole has become more difficult.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The workload of the Police has shot up tremendously with the explosion of tech-related crime and scams all over the world, including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Criminals enabled by technology, are getting smarter too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With the transnational nature of most crime, solving cases and recovering stolen proceeds has become much more complex.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Dark webs provide safe havens to conduct illicit transactions without being detected.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is, therefore, no wonder that the dollar value of crime is continuing to shoot up.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My understanding is that the subject matter value of the cases for 2022 and 2023 continues to be high.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Against this backdrop, our officers naturally will have to be better resourced to match not just these operational challenges but to deal with future threats too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How does the Home Team plan to do this?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When giving the figures above, the Minister frankly admitted that this is not a sustainable situation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He also said that the performance and effectiveness of the force may deteriorate as a result.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Should that happen, there will have an impact on our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Coming from the hon Minister, this is a red flag.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When he shared his view, it brought back memories of my service as a regular in the Police Force in the investigation branch of a division in the early 1990s.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Investigating Officers (IOs) had 24-hour shifts, which meant they were on duty for about 36 hours at a stretch.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The next day, they reported for work during office hours and this cycle repeated itself every three days.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I believe hon Members who also served around the same time as I, such as Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Patrick Tay, would have undergone similar experiences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have seen officers who could not cope with such high demands of their jobs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They accumulated more than 100 Investigation Papers per person and just got bogged down.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Certainly, their morale and well-being suffered as a result.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I recently had a chance to speak to an ex-colleague who retired as a Station Inspector.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His daughter is serving in the Police Force.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I recalled how proud he was when his daughter decided to follow his footsteps to join the men and women in blue.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He shared that almost every day – for a long period of time – his daughter has been working feverishly, often well beyond midnight.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This has gone on to an extent where he is now actively advising his daughter to resign because as a father, he is concerned about her mental wellness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Coming from a decorated retired-Police officer, this is significant.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whilst they are still relatively small, the numbers are trending up and have almost tripled from 2.06% in 2020 to 5.78 % in 2022.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Anecdotally, I understand that the turnover figure for 2023 remains elevated.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful if the hon Minister could share the latest turnover figures.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Part of the reason is because the private sector is able to attract these officers with higher pay and better work conditions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I accept that Home Team officers are a special breed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Home Team officers also know that: as uniformed officers charged with the responsibility of keeping our country safe and secure, they are expected to make sacrifices in the discharge of their duty to our country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Nonetheless, the combination of high workload of the Home Team officers and the lure of the private sector constitutes, in my view, a warning sign on the ability of the Home Team to attract and retain talent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It would be prudent to tackle these issues sooner rather than later.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to ask the hon Minister how does the Home Team intend to address its manpower constraints?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given the tight manpower situation across all sectors in Singapore, I accept that this is not an easy issue to resolve but we have no choice but to double down our efforts on this front.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our security and safety as a nation, depends on ensuring that our Home Team has an adequately sized force.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We also need to ensure the well-being of our officers and not to constantly overload them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Can the hon Minister please give some details about the efforts to recruit and retain officers in the past few years?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Since 2015, the Home Team has invested heavily in technology to enhance its operational effectiveness and productivity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The technology card however, should not be overplayed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Home Team, on a daily basis, interfaces with our community.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How can it ensure that it retains its human touch when interfacing with the community?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How will the Home Team enhance its service delivery to make these services more accessible, efficient and convenient for members of the public?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I understand that there are other Singapore residents who are publicly known to be associated with foreign political organisations, but have not been designated as PSPs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, I would like to request for more details of the Ministry's criteria for designating PSPs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How does the Ministry assess the risk of foreign interference and the public interest in applying FICA's measures to PSPs?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What are the factors that distinguish Mr Chan from other persons who engage in similar activities but who are not designated as PSPs?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Just a day after that, Minister of State Dr Faishal Ibrahim, in replying to a question relating to LTVP for foreign spouses had said that such applications were assessed individually and holistically and elaborated on some of the factors that are taken into consideration, including length of marriage, the sponsor's ability to financially support the applicant, among others.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Caregiving needs were mentioned as a unique consideration.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I have appealed for many of my Singaporean residents who are married to foreigners and many of them come from less well off households.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is a stressful process and the financial cost are challenging for them, even if they are relatively affordable for most Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I can appreciate that MHA and the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) have to consider many factors in determining whether a LTVP application is approved or not.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Pre-marriage LTVP Assessment (PMLA) is a useful tool, but it has its limitations.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is perfectly understandable, since the officers of the Ministry interface with the public daily and in critical ways, be it calls for police service or investigations, paramedic and ambulance services, immigration matters and others.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The relevance of proper staffing levels is not just a matter of maintaining staff morale.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would be useful if the Ministry could explain whether the manpower crunch is getting worse and if so, what the main reasons are.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: No doubt, within that time, the population in Singapore has increased too, by about 8%.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From 5.47 million in 2014 to 5.92 in June last year, an increase of 450,000 people.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Besides population increase, what are the drivers that add to manpower shortfalls?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How much of this is due to new demands, for example, the formation of new land divisions such as Woodlands Police Division, or new specialised units such as the Anti-Scam Command.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Within the functions that the Police retain and do not outsource, there is acknowledgment that the workload has increased dramatically.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: MHA has highlighted that the preponderance of scam cases has added significantly to the load of Police investigators.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the ground, it is not uncommon to hear from our residents that the investigator for their case has resigned or that there has been a change of investigators, which would add to delays in the investigations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for other public services such as Neighbourhood Police establishments, the trend has been to leverage on technology so as to reduce manpower demands.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While I accept that this is necessary, has the Ministry assessed the public satisfaction levels for such changes, especially in the elderly population?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For officers who have resigned, some may have done so due to pull factors such as better prospects elsewhere.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Ministry share what proportion of resignations were due to push factors, such as workload or high public expectations?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Outsourcing of police functions to auxiliary police officer (APO) or private security is logical and a necessary strategy to overcome manpower shortfalls.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Overall, I do see that the outsourcing moves over the years have been incremental and deliberate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By that, I mean that the nature of the task is assessed first to be potentially capable of being outsourced, then training of the auxiliary police or private security will be done before the outsourcing is effective.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, over the years, we see many modular courses being offered in security screening, crowd and traffic control, threat observation and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is common these days to see APO escorting prisoners and manning our land checkpoints, or private security officers deployed at major events.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, there must be some limits to outsourcing, as some tasks are probably too complex, are too risky or require the exercise of discretion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During the recent debate on the amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code, I voiced my concern about whether APOs should be deemed authorised officers for the purpose of exercising force to extract a forensic specimen from an uncooperative criminal suspect.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the Ministry of Law replied that they would be trained for this, this to me, is a confrontational task that carries high risk.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In making decisions on outsourcing, there are legal accountability issues to consider as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If say, a police officer acts wrongly or negligently, being a public servant, the Government is potentially liable for his acts as an employer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is a reassurance to the public that losses can be recovered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the case of an APO or private security officer, a private employer is vicariously liable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While companies providing APO services are well resourced, many private security agencies are not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was further recognised that letting non-Singaporeans carry firearms was a risk which would be managed through security screening, training and supervision.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Ministry elaborate a little on the reasons for the selection of the four Asian jurisdictions?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does proficiency in certain languages play a part?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And if so, I am wondering why countries such as Nepal have not been named.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am supportive of the Government's efforts in recent years to uplift and transform the private security industry.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the national level, with a better trained private security workforce, there will be better cost efficiencies through utilising the workforce from both the public and private sectors and right-sizing them to the task at hand.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the ground level, we see the growth of security providers with better operational capabilities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Many of our residents also work as security officers and are enjoying higher salaries through regulatory requirements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A key driver of these changes is the Security Industry Transformation Map (ITM) launched in 2018.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In response to a PQ I filed in 2021, the Ministry reported that significant progress had been made on the four pillars of the ITM.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Of particular interest to me is the first pillar, namely, to push for technology and innovation to transform operating models.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The aim of such technology adoption is to achieve manpower efficiencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe it is still common to have 12-hour shifts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, are younger people considering such a career?

speaker: The Chairman
text: You have five cuts, you may take your five cuts together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Elevating security personnel to skilled professionals is essential to strengthening public safety and confidence in the face of emerging security challenges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In view of this, my questions are: What impact will the Security Industry Transformation Map 2025 have on the professionalism and skill development of security personnel?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Will both security and non-security personnel within organisations/facilities receive training on the Threat-Oriented Person Screening Integrated System (TOPSIS)?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: What strategies are in place to recruit and retain suitably qualified personnel across the security industry?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Racial harmony is essential for Singapore's peace and stability, fostering mutual respect and deterring tensions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In terms of managing the differences, a study conducted by The Institute of Policy Studies study in 2019 revealed that younger generations prefer community-driven approaches.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: They responded positively to dialogue and community efforts to address racial or religious issues, reflecting their sensitivity to discrimination and willingness to challenge prejudices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In view of this, my questions are: How will the proposed new Maintenance of Racial Harmony Act reflect the importance of dialogue and understanding to promote racial harmony?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: How will the proposed new Maintenance of Racial Harmony Act reflect "gentler measures" and "persuasion and rehabilitation" to assist resolve racial issues?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Is the Ministry considering incorporating the principles and practices of restorative justice in the proposed new Maintenance of Racial Harmony Act to assist resolve racial issues?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: And finally, what avenues do Singaporeans have to peacefully and publicly express their views on domestic and international issues, including the Israel-Hamas conflict?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Supporting offenders' rehabilitation during incarceration decreases reoffending upon release, promoting safer communities and reducing the burden on the criminal justice system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Incorporating trauma-informed care, desistance theory and restorative justice practices into rehabilitation is vital for holistic healing, positive behaviour change and successful reintegration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In view of this, my questions are: What strategies are in place to incorporate the suggested theories into rehabilitation and reintegration programmes for inmates, ex-offenders and their families?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: What are the key outcomes to date from the new Inter-Ministry Committee formed in 2023 to address rising levels of drug use among young people?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Supporting these victims is crucial, as they suffer financial losses, emotional distress and psychological trauma.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By providing assistance, we aid in their recovery, restore security, and offer resources for support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In view of this, my questions are: what programmes are in place to support victims of scams?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Community plays a crucial role in combating scams in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By raising awareness, educating individuals, and fostering vigilance, we empower the community to identify and prevent scams effectively.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: What programmes are in place to enhance the community's interest and capacity to detect, prevent and report scams and cybercrimes?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In the Ministerial Statement on 6 February 2024, the Ministry highlighted several initiatives and support mechanisms to address the wellbeing of Home Team officers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In view of this, would the Ministry consider establishing clear policies, procedures and mechanisms to protect the privacy, confidentiality, and job security of Home Team Officers who choose to seek mental health support?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider establishing an anonymous reporting system that would enable Home Team Officers to seek and obtain private and confidential mental health support, without fear of reprisal?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: And in view of the integration of technology into law enforcement, how will the integration of technology into law enforcement enhance the effectiveness of policing, improve public safety, promote community policing and support front line officers to manage their workload?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The whole investigation process can be complex and requires an eye for detail as well as skills in preparing and presenting evidence.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As a lawyer who takes up criminal matters from time to time, I have seen that our SPF IOs are competent and do a good job collecting evidence and assisting the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC).

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, investigations take some time; but this is understandable given the increasing complexity of crimes, including cybercrimes.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I note that the number of physical crimes has remained stable but that the number of scams has risen significantly.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On a related note, I agree with the hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim and I would like to join her in calling on the SPF to consider engaging private investigators (PIs) to assist in the work of SPF IOs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: PIs are trained and have experience precisely in doing so and their contributions have been invaluable in civil suits.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the Ministry could consider availing of their expertise in criminal investigations as well?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And on a related note, perhaps the SPF can also consider engaging security agencies to outsource some of their functions – their security-related functions to them as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I just wanted to clarify that in my speech, I did not call for outsourcing of Police investigations to private investigators.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: I think it was engaging PIs to do some of these works.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, do you want to further clarify?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, my speech was actually about outsourcing, but it did not specifically call for investigations to be outsourced because I did mention that I considered it to be a rather high-risk activity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, just to clarify: I did not call for that.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Chairperson, officers serving in the Home Team are friends of our citizens today.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: A good example is the Neighbourhood Policing System.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Civil Defence Force has opened its doors and held open houses at many of its fire stations.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The Home Team is people-centric and with this comes a higher expectation of service delivery standards – be it at a 999 or a 995 call or at service centres.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: My question for the Ministry is what plans does the Home Team have to enhance its service delivery to make these services more accessible for the public?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Home Team is facing a plethora and spectrum of challenges with the growing complexity of crimes exacerbated by the speed of digitalisation, technology and GenAI.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the same vein, I wanted to get an update on the rollout of SPF's suite of services to enhance service delivery to members of the public and to develop the next generation of officers to be equipped with new competencies and capabilities to stand ready, relevant and resilient – ready with the new skills and training, relevant to the redesigned jobs and tasks and resilient to the many curve balls and changes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In this regard, I suggest that all of MHA's agencies especially SPF, SCDF and SPS explore even greater partnerships with stakeholders and the community to achieve its goals and mission.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I further submit that we should also find ways to engage the services of ex-Home Team officers – who may have left service long ago or retired from service – to support and take up some of the roles of those in active service to alleviate the manpower crunch.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, there are many Singaporeans who continue to feel strongly about the conflict and are looking for way to express their views and emotions.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While Singaporeans may be able to understand the Government's foreign policy position, one has only to look to social media to see the outpouring of reactions amongst Singaporeans about the devastation that has been inflicted on Gaza.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This has not abated and may even have increased as the conflict continues to rage on.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Influencers have also been reported in the press as having been approached or questioned by authorities on their activism about the conflict.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There is still clearly very strong sentiment on the ground about the conflict.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In his 2021 National Day Rally speech, the Prime Minister announced that the Ministry will be introducing a Maintenance of Racial Harmony Act.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This law is meant to include "softer" measures that can order someone who has caused offence to stop doing it and to make amends by learning more about the other race concerned with a view to mending ties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: However, this harmony did not come by accident.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In the 1960s for example, Singapore experienced race riots between the Chinese and Malay communities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Since then, we have taken steps to build a cohesive society, including with unique measures like ethnic quotas for public housing – to ensure different races live together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In relation to religious harmony, we have had the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act in place for more than 30 years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This gives authorities the power to take pre-emptive measures against those that threaten our religious harmony and a variety of powers to prosecute and deal with those who commit offences under the act.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Interestingly, while we often talk of racial and religious harmony in the same breath, we do not have similar legislation in place to deal with racial harmony.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: One explanation for this may be that religion built around organisations and there was a need to deal with religious organisations in a systematic way.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The Israel-Hamas conflict has been a matter that has evoked strong emotions amongst many of us.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Yet, the sympathy for the Palestinian cause is also strong and Singapore and many of our citizens believe in a two-state solution.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: As the conflict is escalating, the death and damage in Palestine and the mounting civilian death toll has been staggering.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singaporeans have been vocal on this issue, but sympathies are divided; and it appears sometimes along religious and communal lines.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This was also evident in recent reactions to how this matter was being discussed in the Singapore schools.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Deep divisions like this may threaten religious and racial harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Related to this, in some other countries, there have been public protests and demonstrations related to the Israel-Hamas conflict.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Given the strong views that people have on this matter, it may be helpful to have healthy outlets where people can share views on this matter and remain safe.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Does MHA have any guidance or suggestions on this front?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim, you have two cuts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is also coming into the fifth month since the war and humanitarian crisis in Gaza unfolded.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Wars are not just between physical combatants, but the battlegrounds are increasingly fought in the cyberspace as well to capture the minds and hearts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is thus possibility for disinformation campaigns by non-state actors which aim to destabilise and sow divisions in societies.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore's susceptibility to foreign influences and fake news is a pressing concern – particularly in the context of such global conflicts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a multicultural and globally connected society, Singapore is inevitably exposed to diverse perspectives and information from around the world.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It becomes imperative for Singaporeans to exercise critical thinking, verify sources and seek balanced perspectives to navigate the influx of information responsibly.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I want to thank our MHA security officers who have worked tirelessly day in and day out to monitor our regional and national security situation and keep us safe.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In recent years, there is a concerning trend globally of increasing lax attitudes towards drugs among youths.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Despite Singapore's strict anti-drug policies and extensive educational campaigns, we need to safeguard against this attitude creeping among our younger demographics.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Factors, such as peer influence, social media glamorisation and a perception of drugs as recreational substances rather than harmful narcotics, contribute to this worrying shift in attitudes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Previously, I spoke in this House on how – globally – drug cartels and certain drug lobbyists are specifically targeting youths and young professionals.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, for those who have fallen to the trap of drug abuse, we need to help our desistors in terms of emotional, financial and social support so that they can remain steadfast in their path towards recovery, rehabilitation and reintegration; and not fall towards recidivism and fall back to crime and drugs.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Where we rightly double down in our fight against drugs, global and regional trends suggest a more permissive attitude towards drug use and drug abusers are starting younger.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to ask ourselves, how is it that teenagers as young as 14 years old – as reported by the Singapore Drug Situation Report – have access to these drugs?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It cannot be that they just suddenly develop the habit and achieve access to these substances.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond the quantitative the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) statistics released thus far, I urge MHA to have a deeper look at the qualitative aspects of each case to study the social determinants that lead to drug use and target these proximal factors better – as part of a whole-of-Government approach.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: And to look deeper at community prevention strategies with other ministries, community partners and the National Addictions Management Service to better strategise a broader, wrap-around approach in its drug prevention efforts in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Preventive drug education and teaching drug harms in schools need a better approach, for we must protect our young robustly from having access to these substances.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I also wonder whether the numbers of new psychoactive substances are an underestimation, because they can be harder to detect in standard detection kits.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Where there is money to be made, scammers are ruthless in baiting and ensnaring individuals in their moment of vulnerability and when they least suspect it.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: And victims – having been scammed – are often encumbered with guilt and shame, as well as the incredulity and disbelief after.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Where there is money to be made, scammers are ruthless in baiting and ensnaring individuals in their moment of vulnerability and when they least suspect it.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: And victims, having been scammed, are often encumbered with guilt and shame, as well as the incredulity and disbelief after.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Recent figures released by SPF show a continued rise in scam numbers and that more and more people are falling prey to scammers.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It does not reassure us that scammers continue to be guile and creative in their ways and equip themselves with the technology to scale scamming operations remotely to find their next unsuspecting victim and scam to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars per year.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It suggests a knowledge gap in the public and a lack of general vigilance and awareness of the potential of being scammed.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: We also do not want people to feel so paralysed that they retreat inwards and not avail themselves to the use of technology that could make their lives easier.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Can MHA elaborate how the Ministry intends to strengthen its approach to prevent scams at the population level and share the breakdown of scam victims by demographic indicators?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Are there specific vulnerable age groups and communities that need more help?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Earlier this month, three teenage girls were arrested for abusing Ice, two of them were 13 years old.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The increase amongst youths and at a younger age is a worrying development.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This is despite education campaigns against drugs in schools, along with the constant and consistent reminders on the dangers of abusing drugs.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: About a fifth of those who had taken drugs did so because they were curious about the illicit substances.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Other reasons were the belief that the drugs would help with their problems and also from being influenced by friends.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In the third quarter of 2023, the Inter-Ministry Committee on Drug Prevention for Youths was formed to look into developing a whole-of-Government response to the drug problem amongst youths, with a focus on drug prevention.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Ministry and the Government share on the efforts made since and, if it not too soon, how effective some of these responses have been?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Can we also improve the recidivism rate through a relooking of the process for a drug abuser's treatment and journey of rehabilitation and reintegration?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The prevalence of scams in our society has been an increasing source of concern.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: These are, essentially, cheating and stealing in this digital age.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This was despite numerous media warnings, education and new measures.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We are now aiming to grow digital literacy amongst our seniors to perform their daily activities, access digital Government services, manage their health on mobile apps and make electronic payments.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Current statistics do not show seniors as a major group of victims of scams.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This could shift as more seniors embrace technology.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Government share what efforts are in place and planned to protect seniors from scams?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: How will we actively engage seniors to stay alert to new scams potentially targeted at this group while helping them to embrace technology with confidence?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The situation is compounded by the continued emergence of new psychoactive substances (NPS) as well as the increasingly rampant use of vaporisers.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Against this backdrop, can MHA elaborate on its plans to engage other agencies, schools and parents more effectively to identify at-risk youths for timelier intervention?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: What are MHA's new plans to disrupt the supply of such substances targeting our youths and to curb online misinformation that wrongly promotes liberal drug use attitudes?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In my interactions with inmates during our Every Worker Matters conversations, I realise we stand at a critical crossroads in the journey toward a fair and just society, a society that not only punishes the wrongdoer but also strives to rehabilitate and reintegrate those who have paid their debt to society.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: As we consider the fate of ex-offenders re-entering our communities, we are confronted with a moral imperative to provide them with the support and resources necessary to become more productive members of society once more.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: We collectively recognise that the cycle of crime and punishment cannot be broken through punitive measures alone.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: We must invest in programmes that aid in the reintegration of ex-offenders, providing them with the tools they need to secure employment, housing and a sense of dignity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: By doing so, we not only reduce recidivism rates but also foster a more compassionate and inclusive society.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, you have three cuts, you can take them together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My first cut is about drugs and deterring recreational cannabis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Last year, we amended our Misuse of Drugs Act to increase the punishments for possession of selected controlled drugs above certain weight thresholds, which include cannabis, cannabis mixture and cannabis resin.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a very good step and a necessary one, given the severity of its impact on society and especially our young.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as we fight the battle to help our young people battle their mental health issues, we must take a very strong stance on cannabis and other drugs from entering our borders or being accessible by anyone, but especially young people.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our young people are heavily influenced by social media and the global shift in public attitudes has led to more countries not only legalising medical use but also the recreational use of cannabis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, I would like to pause and use as an example the case of Thailand.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is an example which I was quite alarmed at a few years ago when I visited Thailand with my family.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There were pop-up shops of cannabis being sold to general tourists.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: You could smell the whiff of cannabis in the air.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: You fast forward a year or two, there seems to have been a U-turn.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, let me share with the House that, in particular, Thailand decriminalised the cannabis plant in June 2022 with the purpose of supporting medical use and research purposes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the outcome of the decriminalisation ended up allowing young people, especially those under 18, to become cannabis abusers with a sharp increase in usage.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The findings have spurred or looked to have spurred Thailand's Justice Minister to call for a classification of cannabis as a narcotic substance until proper regulation can be put into place.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thailand's arguable quick reversal, not more than two years after decriminalisation, shows how rampant the drug abuse problem can become among young people.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must never let this happen in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have spoken about this multiple times and I think we should not let an example like this go unnoticed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have to continually enforce strong laws against drugs and keep up to speed with developments and ensure our legislation is flexible and adaptable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There will also be pro-cannabis groups with commercial interests who want to influence the narrative surrounding recreational cannabis by diminishing youth's perception of its harm and we have to be active in countering such a view.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For those who are young, they have much potential if given the right environment to rehabilitate and allow them to make choices to walk away from drugs and never return.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They need the love and support of their family and friends and the wider community.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The statistics surrounding repeat offenders show that despite our strict laws, those who have served their jail time continue to be placed in an environment where they have made the choice to re-offend.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Building support in our community to come alongside former offenders is a national effort.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Yellow Ribbon Project and the song which its namesake emphasises, that the idea of welcoming home those who have been to prison, that while offenders can be released from prison, the key to unlocking them from social stigma lies, first, in their families and loved ones and us as society to welcome them back and give them that chance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond familial support, we can look to education and employment as well.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as we intensify our preventive drug education through Government agencies, community groups and anti-drug advocates, we must also educate on how to support and include former offenders so that they can move on.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This education on support must come alongside promoting drug-free values and lifestyles so as to not unintentionally introduce prejudice and stigma.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead, we can inculcate drug-free values at the same time that we introduce values, such as compassion and mercy, which give the public a holistic picture of our battle against drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That same lens can be taken by employers in giving former offenders a second or third, or even possibly, a fourth chance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The prevalence of scams and its impact need no reiterating.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Billions have been lost in tens of thousands of cases in the past few years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It gives rise to the need for the twin pillars of prevention and education.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In seeking to reinforce our blockage of preventing scams, it is pertinent to look to other jurisdictions in this global fight.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the UK – as part of its fraud strategy – they are restructured to allow for cross-sector work to focus on scams.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This allows for sharing of information across the banking and finance sectors on emerging threats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Data breaches and compromised card details; as well as blocking high-risk advertisements and numbers spoofing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally building an infrastructure and legislative regime that would allow for responsibility to be shared among the right actors would bring about cooperative incentives to address the current lapses.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While individuals who fall prey to scams should have their level of individual responsibility – the burden cannot be entirely borne by them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The right allocation would allow for the right resources to be allocated to combat scams.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: At that time, the statistics released by the Police on scams in 2022 produced worrying numbers.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, the increase in the number of scams overall is surely a deeply worrying statistic.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Based on the numbers – while each scam victim may have lost less than in previous years, there has been a significant increase in the number of Singaporeans falling for scams.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This means that more and more Singaporeans are falling for scams in one way or another.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: One of the items in the Police Report that caught my attention was the Police's concern about the sharp increase in the number of scams that are perpetuated through social media and messaging platforms.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I understand that part of this trend includes fraudulent advertisements that are placed on social media platforms.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As consumers, we place a certain level of trust on paid advertisements that are circulated by reputable organisations.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We certainly do not expect to encounter advertisements in the Straits Times, Zaobao, Berita Harian or the Tamil Murasu to be fraudulent or phishing advertisements.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We must therefore surely expect the same from reputable social media platforms, given the fact that they are profiting from these fraudulent advertisements placed on their platforms.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: A simple extrapolation – the more successful scam ads are on social media platforms, scammers will place more of such ads – leading to increased advertising revenue for the platforms.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In such cases, we should look into ways to hold such social media platforms accountable for such scam ads when Singaporeans fall prey to them.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Overall Madam, I am sure that all of us hear many anecdotal stories from residents who seek our assistance when they are scammed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: When a line of attack is foiled, one or two others seemed to emerge.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The threat of scams and the harm it brings to those scammed is insidious and significant.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I hope that the Government will take steps to augment the powers of the Police, by legislation or otherwise, work with the private-sector partners, such as our financial institutions, social media platforms and other stakeholders, in the process to combat scams and protect the community.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the premise, I invite the Minister to share with this House, the steps that the Government is taking to address the threat of scams in the community: whether the Ministry has plans to strengthen legislation to combat scams; and importantly, the efforts that are made to educate and keep the public informed of the latest developments so that Singaporeans can take the necessary precautions against scams?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We should uphold this reputation in the digital sphere too – so our residents and businesses can truly thrive within.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: MHA has made significant strides in fighting scams.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: From the Anti-Scam Command to the ScamShield app and new legislation, such as the Online Criminal Harms Act, they reflect MHA's commitment to enhancing its capabilities against scams.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I previously emphasised the importance of having a concerted "all-hands-on-deck" approach by every stakeholder in the digital ecosystem, which has been crucial in preventing worser outcomes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I commend the combined efforts of MHA, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, banks and telecom companies in reducing phishing scams and swiftly reduced malware scams.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, scams that account for the majority of cases and biggest losses are those that exploit victims' emotions and psychology, for them to authorise and willingly part with their money.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: These include jobs, e-commerce and fake friend scams.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While public vigilance is key to deal with the scourge of scams, our agencies must be more proactive too in monitoring and analysis – to be even more agile and responsive towards new exploitative scam typologies together with partners.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: One, given the success of the Anti-Scam Command in working with banks to stem the flow of monies from phishing scams, will MHA consider establishing similar partnerships with platform companies, such as Meta and Carousell, to swiftly disrupt and investigate tainted e-commerce and messaging accounts?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Two, how can MHA be even more proactive in leveraging trends and insights for smarter deployment of anti-scam resources, to pre-empt and mitigate exploitative scam types?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: For example, the expectation of concert ticket scams related to a foreseeably high-demand performance; or job scams related to popular job categories or activities that seem to earn easy money.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Three, what are new plans and strategies MHA will adopt to further equip the SPF and related agencies to deal with scams perpetrated by new technologies, such as AI?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of these scams have been conducted via platforms and channels like Facebook, Telegram, WhatsApp, Carousell and other e-commerce sites.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will MHA work with online platforms to better protect Singaporeans from scams?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will MHA be reviewing its public education strategy to improve its reach and effectiveness for the prevention of online scams?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Online scams are a scourge affecting not just Singapore, but also many other countries.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many lives and families have been wrecked by this growing digital pandemic.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Scams in other forms are equally problematic – causing financial hardships, undermining the social fabric and eroding public trust in societies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: MHA's budget has grown over the years and that has allowed us to build up the Home Teams' capabilities – so that we can deal with security challenges more effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have many challenges and those challenges evolve.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will touch on three issues – the scam situation in Singapore; drug abuse among youths, especially cannabis; and the resourcing of the Home Team.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And my fellow officeholders will deal with the other points raised by Members of Parliament (MPs).

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In terms of overall safety and security, Singapore continues to rank well in international assessments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the World Justice Project Rule of Law Index 2023, we were ranked one of the top three countries in the "Order and Security" category – for the seventh time in a row.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our physical crime and drug situation has remained relatively stable and under control.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Several MPs have asked about the Ministry's efforts to combat scams.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, the speed and convenience of online transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Scammers can reach out to potential victims easily.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They can move stolen funds quickly and they can hide behind the anonymity of the internet.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second major challenge is that most scammers operate from overseas, beyond our jurisdiction.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Once the monies leave Singapore, it is very difficult, if at all possible, to recover them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the most effective way to tackle scams is really to prevent them from taking place at all.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In this regard, the Government works with stakeholders to strengthen our communications and banking channels, our digital systems and our online platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For instance, telecom companies now block likely scam calls and SMSes from reaching victims in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Banks have introduced new banking features to secure monies in bank accounts, such as the "Kill Switch" and the "Money Lock".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Government agencies and banks have upgraded our e-services to protect users from malware scams.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: MHA is also progressively operationalising the Online Criminal Harms Act, or OCHA.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: OCHA will allow the Government to require designated online platforms to put in place stronger safeguards against scams and other criminal activities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have also strengthened what we can do, post-incident.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Police Anti-Scam Command, or ASCom, works with more than 100 partners, including financial institutions and online platforms, to combat scams.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Staff from financial institutions are co-located with the ASCom, and that allows us to trace and freeze funds and trace and freeze accounts quickly before they are gone.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Last year, we also amended the CDSA, which is the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act, and the CMA, which is the Computer Misuse Act, to make it easier to punish money mules and those who abuse Singpass.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: MHA will also be introducing new laws next month to punish the abuse of local SIM cards for scams.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Government has done what it can do.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It continues to explore other measures to protect the public from scams.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But there is a limit to what we can do.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There is not a single magic bullet, an ironclad shield against scams, unless we roll back digitalisation, which means no more Internet shopping, no smartphones and social media, no Internet banking.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The key line of defence – the critical line of defence – has got to be every individual who has to guard himself or herself, friends, families from scams, and, together with all the other efforts by the Government, banks and other partners, it may be possible to put up a better barrier.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Government has also been conducting extensive public awareness campaigns – and the Minister of State, Sun Xueling, will elaborate on that in her speech.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the last decade, there has been an increase in the global push to decriminalise and legalise drugs consumption.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will be delivering a Ministerial Statement later this year, where I will speak in more detail on the drug situation around the world and our approach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Today, I will focus on our response to the youth drug problem.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Minister of State Faishal Ibrahim will be elaborating on our other measures to combat drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi, Mr Keith Chua and Mr Derrick Goh, as well as Assoc Prof Razwana Begum have raised concerns about the rising number of young drug abusers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They asked about our plans to deal with this problem.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Just earlier this month three Singaporean girls, aged 13 and 14, were arrested for taking drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: An IMH survey published last year also found that many Singaporeans start abusing drugs before the age of 16.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Also, as Mr Christopher de Souza highlighted, cannabis is of particular concern.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It was the third most-commonly abused drug overall and the second most commonly abused drug amongst new drug abusers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Of the new cannabis abusers arrested last year, more than 60% were young people under 30.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There is a slightly more permissive attitude amongst our younger people towards drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are sometimes influenced by what they read and see online, the lifestyles promoted by permissive cultures and societies, and the falsehoods that are peddled.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Arguments for cannabis legalisation are often driven by parties with commercial interests.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They say that cannabis is a harmless soft drug.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They even suggest that it can benefit those who consume it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, I will update Members on the Home Team's transformation efforts and our vision for the future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MHA started our Home Team Transformation journey back in 2015.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We recognised then, the need for the Home Team to prepare for more challenges ahead.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since its introduction in 2016, the cameras have helped our officers focus on doing their jobs well rather than be distracted by malicious allegations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members may recall the incident in 2021 where Police officers were alleged to have bullied an elderly woman.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Camera footage showed beyond any doubt that this was untrue and that the officers were, in fact, helping the woman, who suffered from dementia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since then, we have embarked on BWC 2.0.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The cameras are now even more compact, with longer battery life and live-streaming capability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This improves officers' situational awareness and helps officers make better-informed decisions to manage incidents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the next phase of the Home Team's transformation, we will focus our efforts in four areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, strengthening our operational capabilities, which Mr Patrick Tay and Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim asked about.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To stay ahead of the changing threat landscape, we need to improve our sense-making capabilities, to detect threats earlier, respond faster and better.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Police cameras, or PolCams, are a good example of how we can do that.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In some incidents, footage, aided by video analytics, have enabled the Police to identify, locate and apprehend the suspects involved within hours of a crime being reported.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members may recall that physical harassment by unlicensed moneylenders was once a major concern.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2012, there were more than 7,600 reports of such property damage.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also expand coverage across more locations island-wide.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: SPF and HTX will also deploy autonomous patrol robots to serve as additional eyes on the ground and project Police presence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These patrol robots will provide live video feeds to the Police's Operations Command Centres.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Officers at the Operations Command Centres will also be able to communicate with members of the public remotely through the patrol robots and provide advice when required.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Home Team will continue to innovate and co-create with industry partners to further our capability building efforts through HTX's new innovation centre, known as Hatch.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Hatch works closely with the Home Team to identify and define key challenges, while simultaneously scouting globally for cutting-edge technologies across diverse sectors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Hatch facilitates direct interactions between startups and the Home Team, providing essential funding and enabling the validation of innovative proof-of-concept (POC) projects through real-world testing and expert guidance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, our second focus is on transforming our operations which Mr Murali Pillai, Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant and Ms Sylvia Lim asked about.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are redesigning our public-facing services so that we can serve Singaporeans more efficiently and still get good security outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The redesign of Neighbourhood Police Centres and the Neighbourhood Police Posts supports SPF's push for digital service delivery to the public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Minister Shanmugam has already explained how they work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are part of SPF's efforts to restructure deployments and optimise resources to serve the community better.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To better manage the surge in travellers, ICA and HTX will be launching the New Clearance Concept at the immigration checkpoints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Contactless clearance will also be introduced, allowing travellers to be identified and cleared via biometrics at the automated lanes, without having to present their passports.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: All Singapore residents, long-term pass holders and departing foreign visitors, will be able to enjoy this hassle-free experience and reduced clearance time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: ICA aims to operationalise its new Services Centre in 2025.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Located beside the current ICA Building, the new Centre provides a single touchpoint to meet the public's multiple immigration needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Documents, such as passports can be collected through self-service kiosks during the Centre's operating hours, without the need to book an appointment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These are part of ICA's efforts to provide the public with a seamless, one-stop "No Fuss, No Visit, No Waiting" experience.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On a separate note, Mr Faisal Manap suggested that ICA creates a streamlined approach to give Singaporeans with foreign spouses more clarity on whether the spouse can qualify for a Long-Term Visit Pass (LTVP).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since 2015, ICA has offered the Pre-Marriage LTVP Assessment (PMLA) to all Singaporeans with foreign spouses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a free online assessment tool to find out if the prospective non-resident spouse is likely to qualify for a LTVP after the marriage.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The application takes no more than 30 minutes and will be processed within one month.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Applicants who have difficulties going online can also approach the ICA's Services Centre or ServiceSG Centres located island-wide.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: From 2021 to 2023, ICA processed an annual average of 4,900 PMLA applications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is an increase over the previous period, likely because of greater awareness through additional touchpoints like the ROM or ROMM as the Member has suggested.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Murali Pillai and Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim asked about the Home Team's efforts to address manpower constraints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is, in fact, our third area of focus.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have been streamlining and automating our internal workflows to free up our officers to focus on more important tasks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Singapore Prison Services (SPS) conducts regular urine tests for both male and female supervisees undergoing Community-based Programmes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, the process of urine collection is both labour-intensive and time-intensive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It requires officers to manually register the supervisee, supervise the urine procurement and conduct drug testing on the sample.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With PASS, a single officer will be able to manage the end-to-end process of urine procurement and testing across multiple cubicles.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will be done in a contactless and fully automated manner, that also provides privacy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition, PASS will leverage technology to interpret the results of the urine tests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Home Team have also been exploring the use of speech-to-text AI technology for transcription of video recorded interviews.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Police is working to streamline the transcription process and will evaluate its usefulness to investigation officers through a trial to be conducted later this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked about the Home Team's efforts to develop the next generation of officers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is our fourth and likely most important area of focus – to train and develop competencies in our officers to ensure that they are future-ready.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One example is the StressVest that SPF has trialled, which is a laser-based simulation system to hone the skills of Police officers in tactical maneuvers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Such systems provide greater realism as they can simulate a range of scenarios, including armed combat.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will better prepare officers to tackle security threats on the ground.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Prisons and HTX are currently trialling an Accuracy and Impact Manikin (AIM) that is able to measure force and zonal impact and will help to assess the accuracy of strikes and the deployment of force.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will enhance the training of our officers in unarmed and defensive tactics and trainers will be able to monitor the progress of each trainee via a dashboard.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Murali Pillai and Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim asked how technology will be used to improve community policing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Home Team is therefore keen to deepen and widen our engagement and partnership with the public and other stakeholders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will use technology to strengthen our officers' engagement with the community, rather than to replace it or diminish it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This can be seen with SPF's Community Engagement Robot, known affectionally as "CODY", which will be deployed during community outreach events.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: CODY will interact with and disseminate crime prevention messages to the public through a wide range of multimedia interactive activities, such as videos, games, quizzes and chats.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: CODY will be accompanied by SPF officers and will enable SPF officers to reach out to more members of the public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will allow the Operations Centre personnel to see what is happening on the ground and to provide the Community First Responders with live guidance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will, in turn, enable the Responders to provide better and more timely interventions in emergency situations, where every second counts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to conclude with some comments in Mandarin.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In Mandarin):   Over the past few years, the Home Team has made good progress in its transformation efforts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the face of increasingly severe challenges in the security environment, we will continue to adopt technology to strengthen our response capabilities, work together to ensure the successful implementation of transformation measures and strive to maintain the public trust in the Home Team.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also understand that some members of the public may feel unfamiliar, or even uneasy, about the rapid advancement of technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Therefore, while leveraging technology, the Home Team will carefully consider its impact on the public, adopt a people-centric design and maintain empathy and human touch when serving the people.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister of State Assoc Prof Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore's safety and security have been achieved in large part, by us staying united and protecting our social cohesion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Many in Singapore have been following the developments in Gaza closely.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: What we have seen has been disturbing: tens of thousands dead, towns completely destroyed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We feel deeply for the many innocent lives lost and hope to see the end of suffering in Gaza soon.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Vikram Nair asked how our different communities have reacted to the conflict.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: How the different communities react will vary according to how they identify with the affected groups in the community.
